source.title: Do We Need Zero Training Loss After Achieving Zero Training Error?
source.authors: Takashi Ishida; Ikko Yamane; Tomoya Sakai; Gang Niu; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests how test accuracy changes with several levels of randomly corrupted labels in synthetic datasets, but does not test fitting completely random labels or the image settings in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports synthetic-data test accuracies at 1%, 5% and 10% label noise. It does not report whether training error reaches zero in those conditions. Results about flooding on clean benchmark datasets do not test the listed random-label claims.
record.test_reason: Table 3 bears on V5's true-label generalization component: networks trained without flooding, early stopping or weight decay still generalize well on MNIST, Kuzushiji-MNIST and SVHN. The study does not establish fitting random labels. Table 2 reports noisy-data test accuracy without corresponding training-fit measurements.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: flooding maintains a small positive training loss, validation-selected flood levels often preserve zero training error, and flooding improves test accuracy in various synthetic and benchmark settings. The authors also report test-loss double descent and a conditional reduction in risk-estimator MSE.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces flooding, which changes the training objective. Its synthetic label-noise experiments use a five-hidden-layer feedforward network with Adam; the benchmark experiments use other architectures and SGD. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: For synthetic data, test accuracy varies with dataset and label-noise level. The paper also compares flooding and early stopping.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports declining test accuracy as synthetic label noise increases. Without flooding or early stopping, accuracy falls from 90.52% to 78.44% for Two Gaussians, 97.72% to 82.38% for Spiral, and 94.62% to 78.47% for Sinusoid between 1% and 10% noise. Training error is not reported, and the noise is described as changing Bayes risk.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test accuracy decreases with increasing label noise in these synthetic classification tasks; flooding often improves accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.1 and Figure 3 show that selected flood levels often preserve zero training error on original-label benchmarks, while larger flood levels reduce training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Positive training loss can coexist with zero training error on original-label datasets.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The synthetic label-noise results report test accuracy but do not report training error for those conditions. Noise levels are limited to 1%, 5% and 10%; the paper does not test completely random labels. Reported accuracies are averages and standard deviations over 10 trials.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the synthetic results in Table 2 report test accuracy under label noise, but do not report training error, so they cannot establish the behavior V4 describes. The benchmark results use original labels and do not test V1–V6.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Memorization of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian-generated synthetic classification data do not establish this.

Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and degradation toward chance from zero to complete corruption. Table 2 supplies only test accuracy at 1%, 5% and 10% noise; the paper describes this noise as changing Bayes risk and does not establish a training-only corruption experiment with clean test labels.

Whether weight decay, dropout and augmentation prevent fitting random labels; removal of dropout; and the isolated effect of removing augmentation, which is bundled with learning-rate decay in Table 3.
Separate learning dynamics for genuine patterns and noisy labels.

missing.what: Extract the true-label weight-decay controls bearing on V5: without flooding or early stopping, MNIST accuracy is 98.45% without versus 98.53% with weight decay; Kuzushiji-MNIST is 92.27% versus 92.21%; SVHN is 92.38% versus 93.20%. The record incorrectly dismisses all benchmark results as irrelevant to V1–V6.

record.verdict_notes: No rows were supplied. The V5 verdict rests on Table 3 and concerns only its true-label generalization component. Table 2's omitted results are already declared in rows_left_out; they do not establish V4's joint memorization-and-generalization behavior.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random versus true labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.

The reported synthetic label-noise results cover only 1%, 5% and 10% noise and report test accuracy, not whether training error remains zero. No image-label corruption sweep from none to all is reported.
Whether weight decay, dropout or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Whether real-data patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Original-label MNIST, Kuzushiji-MNIST and SVHN; without flooding or early stopping; weight-decay controls
relationships.reason: Text/Table 3, with no extracted row ids: accuracy without weight decay is 98.45%, 92.27% and 92.38%, respectively, versus 98.53%, 92.21% and 93.20% with weight decay. These results support the component that omitting weight decay need not make true-label generalization poor.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracies without weight decay were 98.45%, 92.27%, and 92.38%, respectively, versus 98.53%, 92.21%, and 93.20% with it.
